analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil companies on windfall crude-oil profits and rebates the money to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in November 2005 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2007, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have placed a temporary excise tax on large oil companies, taking 50% of the profit on each barrel of crude oil sold above $40 (adjusted for inflation), minus what the company invested in drilling, refineries, or renewable fuel facilities. All of the money collected would have been sent back to taxpayers as a rebate check each February. The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: All eligible taxpayers would receive an annual rebate funded by the tax, with the amount set by the Treasury based on how much revenue the tax raised the previous year [S3]. The rebate is capped at a taxpayer's prior-year tax liability, so it could offset tax owed rather than exceed it [S3]. Households paying high gasoline and heating prices in the wake of 2005's energy price spike stood to get some of that money back, and investments in refineries and renewable fuels were exempted from the tax, so companies that reinvested paid less [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers facing high energy prices

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on integrated oil companies equal to 50% of the windfall profit on each barrel of crude oil above an inflation-adjusted base price of $40, credited for the company's qualified investments in drilling, refineries, and renewable fuel facilities [S2] [S3].

Rebates the tax revenue back to individual taxpayers as a payment deemed made each February 1, with the Treasury setting the amount based on the prior year's collections and the number of taxpayers [S2] [S3].

The tax is temporary: it applies only to crude oil removed within three years of enactment, and oil from wells drilled after enactment is excluded, limiting the tax to profits on already-producing fields [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large integrated oil companies would pay the tax on windfall profits from crude oil they produced [S2] [S3]. Some economists argue such taxes can lead producers to charge more or produce less, which would pass part of the cost to consumers at the pump; the bill's exclusion of newly discovered oil was a partial response to that concern.

drawbacks.text: A windfall profits tax can discourage domestic oil production or be passed through to consumers in higher prices; Congress enacted a similar tax in 1980 and repealed it in 1988 after producers scaled back drilling. This bill attempts to blunt that by exempting newly discovered oil and crediting investments in refineries and renewable fuels, but the tax still applies to every barrel sold above the base price from existing fields [S3].

The rebate is capped at each taxpayer's prior-year tax liability and depends entirely on how much the tax collects, so the payment to any household would be unpredictable and modest relative to what high fuel prices cost them [S3].
The bill allows oil companies to deduct the windfall tax payment from their income taxes, which reduces the effective burden somewhat and lowers net revenue available for rebates [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly returned oil-industry windfall revenue to ordinary taxpayers, a clear transfer from a concentrated industry to the public. Its weaknesses were practical: the tax could partially flow into consumer prices, the rebate would be modest and unpredictable, and the deduction and investment credits softened the hit to producers. It was a targeted response to the 2005 energy price spike, not a structural fix for energy costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on November 2, 2005, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Windfall Profits Rebate Act of 2005 on November 2, 2005, amid high oil and gasoline prices following that year's hurricanes [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation, and no hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill was never acted on again and expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil companies were better off: they never faced the windfall tax, and consumers never received the rebate. The House tax-writing committee, which never considered the bill, kept oil industry tax treatment unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies; the bill never left committee

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 2, 2005; it was her sole sponsorship, with no cosponsors joining [S1] [S4].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 2, 2005 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never became visible; the bill died with one Democratic sponsor alone [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have taken 50% of their profit on each barrel of crude sold above $40 (inflation-adjusted), less their investments in drilling, refineries, and renewable fuels [S2] [S3]. Because the bill died, the tax never took effect and their windfall revenue from the 2005 price spike was untouched.

The bill credited oil companies' investments in refineries, renewable fuel facilities, and ethanol or biodiesel production against the windfall tax, giving those sectors an indirect funding advantage [S3]. The bill's death removed this incentive.
